question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{-y}(\left(x+6\right)-1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2{e}^{-y}(\left(x+6\right)-1) \\ {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(\left(x+6\right)-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x & =\int 2(\left(x+6\right)-1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int 2\left(x+6\right)\,\text{d}x-\int 2\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & ={\left(x+6\right)}^{2}-2\left(x+6\right)+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
{e}^{y}={\left(x+6\right)}^{2}-2\left(x+6\right)+C.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{\left(x+3\right)}{cos}^{2}⁡\left(y+6\right) \\ \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\left(y+6\right)}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{\left(x+3\right)} \\ {sec}^{2}⁡\left(y+6\right)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{\left(x+3\right)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {sec}^{2}⁡\left(y+6\right)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{\left(x+3\right)}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {sec}^{2}⁡\left(y+6\right)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {e}^{\left(x+3\right)}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {sec}^{2}⁡\left(y+6\right)\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{\left(x+3\right)}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\left(y+6\right) & ={e}^{\left(x+3\right)}+C\end{aligned}

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\left(y+2\right){e}^{\left(x+3\right)} \\ \frac{1}{\left(y+2\right)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{\left(x+3\right)}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\left(y+2\right)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{\left(x+3\right)}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{\left(y+2\right)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {e}^{\left(x+3\right)}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{\left(y+2\right)}\,\text{d}y & =\int {e}^{\left(x+3\right)}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|\left(y+2\right)| & ={e}^{\left(x+3\right)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|\left(y+2\right)|={e}^{\left(x+3\right)}+C

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{\left(x-4\right)}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{\left(x-4\right)}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} \\ {y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={\left(x-4\right)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {\left(x-4\right)}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int {\left(x-4\right)}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{2}\,\text{d}y & =\int {\left(x-4\right)}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{{y}^{3}}{3} & =\frac{{\left(x-4\right)}^{3}}{3}+K \\ {y}^{3} & ={\left(x-4\right)}^{3}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3K.$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
{y}^{3}={\left(x-4\right)}^{3}+C.
$$

question.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{5 x^{2} - 5}{y^{2}}.$ Work on an interval where $y\ne 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{5 x^{2} - 5}{y^{2}} \\ (y^{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =5 x^{2} - 5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (y^{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (5 x^{2} - 5)\,\text{d}x \\ \int (y^{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int (5 x^{2} - 5)\,\text{d}x \\ \int (y^{2})\,\text{d}y & =\int (5 x^{2} - 5)\,\text{d}x \\ \int y^2\,\text{d}y & =\int 5x^2\,\text{d}x-\int 5\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{y^3}{3} & =\frac{5x^3}{3}-5x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\frac{y^{3}}{3}=\frac{5 x^{3}}{3} - 5 x+C.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4 x^{2} - 4}{y^{2}} \\ (y^{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4 x^{2} - 4\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (y^{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (4 x^{2} - 4)\,\text{d}x \\ \int (y^{2})\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int (4 x^{2} - 4)\,\text{d}x \\ \int (y^{2})\,\text{d}y & =\int (4 x^{2} - 4)\,\text{d}x \\ \int y^2\,\text{d}y & =\int 4x^2\,\text{d}x-\int 4\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{y^3}{3} & =\frac{4x^3}{3}-4x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\frac{y^{3}}{3}=\frac{4 x^{3}}{3} - 4 x+C.
$$

\begin{aligned}\int (y^{2} + 3)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (6 x^{2} + 1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int (y^{2} + 3)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int (6 x^{2} + 1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int (y^{2} + 3)\,\text{d}y & =\int (6 x^{2} + 1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int y^2\,\text{d}y+\int 3\,\text{d}y & =\int 6x^2\,\text{d}x+\int 1\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{y^3}{3}+3y & =\frac{6x^3}{3}+1x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\frac{y^{3}}{3} + 3 y=2 x^{3} + x+C.
$$
